newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nissan cuts development time to rev up RV sales.
newsitem.headline: Nissan cuts development time to rev up RV sales.

text.p: Nissan Motor Co Ltd said on Tuesday it had introduced a faster system for producing new models that will cut vehicle development time by 40 percent to just 19 months.

Nissan said the move was expected to cut development costs by almost a third and was aimed at boosting its domestic competitiveness in sales of recreational vehicles, a market sector in in which it has lagged its rivals.

The first model to be developed under the new system will hit the showrooms in the second half of this year, and all new models after that will have been developed in the shorter timeframe, the spokesman said.
Nissan, Japan"s second biggest carmaker, said it would then be the world"s first auto manufacturer to cut development time for all its new vehicles to less than 20 months.
"We have started a new method of car development using a shorter development time. The first model (to be made under the new system) will be launched in the latter half of 1997," the spokesman said.
Development time is the gap between completing the design and the start of mass production.

The shorter production period is expected to cut development costs by about 30 percent, the spokesman said. The industry"s current average development time for a new model is about 30 months, he said.
The change is not expected to affect Nissan's overseas operations because the company -- like other leading Japanese carmakers -- handles most product development in Japan.

Under the new system, design and production divisions liaise more closely than before, frequently exchanging design data before a car design is finalised. Nissan said this allows it to establish the production scheme for new models at the same time as the design is completed.

Nissan, which has been lagging rivals such as Honda and Toyota on development of recreational vehicles, said the change would allow it to roll out new models more quickly and be more responsive to market trends.

"We were well behind other makers like Honda on the development of recreational vehicles but we can introduce new models, including recreational models, quickly under the new system," the spokesman said.
Sales of sporty recreational vehicles have been booming in Japan as motorists have tired of sedan varieties.

Nissan has been hoping to achieve a 25 percent share of the domestic vehicle market by the year 2000. Its domestic share fell to a record low of 20.8 percent in calendar 1996, below the previous record low of 21.2 percent in 1994.
Some carmakers produce certain individual models in less than 19 months but not a whole range of new models, Nissan said.
